method_card.title: How to read rhythm from a score
method_card.content:
Section A of the AQA Listening exam can show you up to 12 bars of staff notation and ask questions about what you see. This lesson drills the rhythmic elements you need to decode quickly.

Key facts:

  • Simple time signatures (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): the top number tells you how many beats per bar; the bottom number tells you the value of each beat (4 = crotchet). A crotchet beat can be subdivided into 2 quavers or 4 semiquavers.
  • Compound time signatures (6/8, 9/8, 12/8): the beat is a dotted note. In 6/8 there are 2 dotted-crotchet beats per bar, each split into 3 quavers. In 12/8 there are 4 dotted-crotchet beats.
  • Dotted rhythms: a dot after a note increases its value by half. A dotted crotchet = 1.5 beats; paired with a quaver = 2 beats total.
  • Anacrusis: a note or notes before the first full bar (a pick-up or upbeat). The Mozart Symphony No.40 first subject opens with an anacrusis of two quavers.
  • Note values in order (longest to shortest): semibreve (4 beats) → minim (2) → crotchet (1) → quaver (½) → semiquaver (¼).

The score excerpts below show examples from pieces you have studied. Use them to answer the questions.
steps: Identify the time signature: how many beats per bar? What is the beat value?
Check whether it is simple (top number 2, 3 or 4) or compound (top number 6, 9 or 12).
Look for dots after notes — add half the note's value.
Find any anacrusis — a bar that is shorter than a full bar at the start.

exam_context.frequency: Section A every paper; Section B for Area of Study 1

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt A (Mozart Symphony No.40). What is the time signature?
bronze.explanation: The score shows 4/4 — four crotchet beats per bar. This is the most common time signature in Western music. Mozart's first subject opens with a two-quaver anacrusis before the first full bar.

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro). What does the time signature symbol 'C with a line through it' mean?
options: 2/2 alla breve (2 half-note beats per bar)
bronze.explanation: The symbol is alla breve or 2/2: two minim (half-note) beats per bar. At a fast Allegro tempo, this creates a driven two-in-a-bar feel. It is equivalent to 4/4 but at double the speed of the beat, giving the music more forward momentum.

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt C (Chopin Nocturne). What is the time signature, and how many main beats does it have per bar?
bronze.explanation: 12/8 is a compound quadruple time signature: four main beats per bar (hence 'quadruple'), each subdivided into three quavers (hence 'compound'). This gives the left-hand arpeggios their flowing, lilting three-in-a-beat quality.

bronze.question: Match each note value to how many crotchet beats it lasts.
bronze.explanation: These are the five standard note values. Each halves in duration as you go down the list. A dotted note adds half its value: dotted minim = 3 beats; dotted crotchet = 1.5 beats.

silver.question: Look at Excerpt A (Mozart Symphony No.40). The piece begins with two quavers before the first full bar. What is this called?
silver.explanation: An anacrusis (also called an upbeat or pick-up) is one or more notes at the start of a piece that come before the first complete bar. The Mozart Symphony No.40 first subject famously opens with two quavers leading into the first full bar. These upbeat quavers give the theme its immediate rhythmic momentum.

silver.question: In Excerpt C (Chopin Nocturne, 12/8), how many quavers does each main beat contain?
silver.explanation: In compound time, each beat is a dotted note, subdivided into 3. In 12/8 each main beat is a dotted crotchet = 3 quavers. With 4 beats per bar and 3 quavers per beat, you get 4 × 3 = 12 quavers per bar — hence the '12' in the time signature.

silver.question: Put the following note values in order from longest (most beats) to shortest (fewest beats).
silver.explanation: From longest to shortest: semibreve (4 beats) → minim (2 beats) → crotchet (1 beat) → quaver (½ beat) → semiquaver (¼ beat). Each value is exactly half the duration of the one above it.

gold.question: Look at Excerpt B (Beethoven Symphony No.1 Allegro). What is the effect of using 2/2 alla breve rather than 4/4 for an Allegro movement?
options: It slows the music down by giving it four separate beats to move through.
It creates a lighter, faster two-in-a-bar feel rather than a heavier four-in-a-bar feel, giving the Allegro greater propulsive energy.
It indicates that only the strings should play — woodwind must wait for the 4/4 section.
It means the music must be played twice as slowly as marked.
gold.explanation: Alla breve (2/2) at a fast Allegro tempo means the conductor beats two per bar instead of four. This creates a momentum-driven, energetic feel: the listener 'feels' two large beats sweeping forward rather than four smaller pulses. Beethoven used alla breve in many fast movements to achieve this driving, continuous energy.

gold.question: Compare Excerpt A (Mozart, 4/4) and Excerpt C (Chopin, 12/8). Which statement best explains the difference in rhythmic character between simple and compound time?
options: Simple and compound time are identical — the beat subdivision is the same.
Simple time (4/4) subdivides each beat into 2 equal parts, giving a straight feel; compound time (12/8) subdivides each beat into 3 equal parts, giving a lilting, swinging 'triplet' feel.
Compound time is always faster than simple time.
Simple time is only used in Baroque music; compound time is only used in Romantic music.
gold.explanation: The key difference is the subdivision of the beat. In simple time (4/4) each crotchet beat divides into 2 quavers — creating a straight, even feel. In compound time (12/8) each dotted-crotchet beat divides into 3 quavers — creating a lilting, rolling feel. This is why Chopin's nocturne arpeggios sound so different from Mozart's quaver motif even at the same approximate tempo.

worked_examples.question: Look at Excerpt C (Chopin Nocturne, 12/8). Explain how the time signature affects the character of the left-hand accompaniment.
steps: Step 1 — identify the time signature. The time signature is 12/8 — compound quadruple time. There are 4 main beats per bar, each subdivided into 3 quavers.
Step 2 — describe the left-hand pattern. The left hand plays arpeggiated chords (broken chords): three notes per beat, flowing upwards. Each group of three quavers = one dotted-crotchet beat.

Step 3 — link to character. The three-in-a-beat subdivision creates a lilting, rocking feel — like a gentle triple-feel wave. This gives the accompaniment its flowing, nocturnal quality, quite different from the straight quavers of a 4/4 rhythm.

Full answer. 'The 12/8 time signature creates 4 dotted-crotchet beats per bar, each subdivided into 3 quavers. The left-hand arpeggios fill each beat with 3 flowing notes, creating a lilting, rocking character that gives the Nocturne its gentle, swaying feel.'
